Unit 7 sample answers: 240° = 4π/3; arc s for r=6, θ=π/3 is 2π; sin(3π/4)=√2/2; given cos θ=4/5 in QIV, sin θ=−3/5; period of y=4 sin(πx/6) is 12; y=tan x asymptotes at π/2+kπ.

weeks.prep: Stacking cups (or blocks), ruler. A ball and tape measure for Day 4.
misconceptions: Using n instead of n − 1 in a_n = a₁ + (n − 1)d. Test with n = 1: the formula must give a₁.
Confusing arithmetic (add d) with geometric (multiply by r). Check differences and ratios first.

days.guide: Measure the height of 1, 2, 3, 4 nested cups. Write a recursive rule and an explicit rule. Today's task from the plan: Build a stacking-cup pattern and write recursive and explicit rules. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: A cup stack is 12 cm for 1 cup and grows 1.5 cm per added cup. Give recursive and explicit rules.
questions.a: Recursive: h₁ = 12, hₙ = hₙ₋₁ + 1.5. Explicit: hₙ = 12 + 1.5(n − 1).

days.guide: Model finding d, writing a_n, and finding any term. Today's task from the plan: Find terms and write formulas a_n = a₁ + (n−1)d. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: a₁ = 7, d = 4. Find a₂₀.
Write a formula for 3, 10, 17, ….

days.guide: Model finding r, a_n = a₁r^(n−1), and the link to y = ab^x. Today's task from the plan: Find terms and write formulas a_n = a₁·r^(n−1); connect to exponential functions. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Find a formula and the 8th term of 2, 6, 18, ….

days.guide: Drop a ball from 2 m and measure rebound heights; compute ratios. Also model a savings plan that adds $50/month. Today's task from the plan: Model a savings plan and a bouncing-ball height sequence with real measurement. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: A ball dropped from 2 m rebounds to 60% of its height each time. How high after the 3rd bounce?

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz on sequence formulas. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Is 5, 10, 20, 40 arithmetic or geometric? Give the next term.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) 4, 9, 14, … a₁₅ = 74. 2) explicit for 20, 17, 14: aₙ = 23 − 3n. 3) 3, −6, 12, … aₙ = 3(−2)^(n−1), a₆ = −96. 4) recursive a₁=5, aₙ=2aₙ₋₁ → 5, 10, 20, 40. 5) Which term of 2, 5, 8 … is 62? n = 21. 6) $1,000 earning 5%/yr: aₙ = 1000(1.05)^(n−1) for the start of year n.

weeks.prep: Spreadsheet. Tell the Gauss 1-to-100 story.
misconceptions: Confusing the number of terms with the last term in Σ. Count terms as (top − bottom + 1).
Applying the infinite-series formula when |r| ≥ 1. Such series diverge (no finite sum).

days.guide: Model reading and writing Σ; student evaluates six sums by hand. Today's task from the plan: Write and evaluate sums in sigma notation. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Evaluate Σ_{k=1}^{5} (2k + 1).

days.guide: Write the sum forwards and backwards and add to derive S = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2. Today's task from the plan: Derive Gauss's formula for arithmetic series and apply it. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

Derive S − rS to get S_n = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r). Apply to a loan: payment = P·i/(1 − (1 + i)^(−n)). Today's task from the plan: Derive S_n = a(1−r^n)/(1−r) and apply to mortgage/loan payment problems. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Sum 3 + 6 + 12 + … (8 terms).
Monthly payment on $20,000 at 6%/year for 60 months?

days.guide: Spreadsheet partial sums for r = 1/2, 0.9, 1.1; observe which level off. S = a/(1 − r) when |r| < 1. Today's task from the plan: Explore convergence when |r| < 1 with a spreadsheet. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Does Σ 2(1.1)^n converge?
questions.a: No: r = 1.1 > 1, the sums grow without bound.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test (about 50 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Unit 8 test on sequences and series. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Write 2 + 4 + 6 + … + 40 in sigma notation and evaluate.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 sample answers: 1) a₁₂ of 5, 9, 13: 49. 2) a₇ of 81, 27, 9: 1/9. 3) Σ_{k=1}^{4} k² = 30. 4) sum of first 30 odd numbers = 900. 5) 1 + 3 + 9 + … + 3⁶ = 1,093. 6) 12 − 6 + 3 − … infinite = 12/(1.5) = 8. 7) Explain why 1 + 2 + 4 + … has no sum. Rubric: formula (1), substitution (1), answer (1).

weeks.prep: Two or three recent news articles that report on a study (health or education topics work well). A random number generator (random.org or a calculator).
misconceptions: Concluding cause and effect from an observational study. Only a randomized experiment can support causation; observational studies show association.
Thinking a larger sample fixes bias. A huge convenience sample is still biased; how you sample matters more than how many.

days.guide: Define survey, experiment (treatment imposed), observational study (no treatment imposed). Student classifies 12 descriptions. Today's task from the plan: Classify 12 study descriptions as surveys, experiments, or observational studies. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Researchers compare heart health of people who already drink coffee with those who don't. Which type?
questions.a: Observational study: no treatment was assigned.

questions.q: Students are randomly assigned to study with or without music. Which type?
questions.a: Experiment: researchers impose the treatment with random assignment.

days.guide: Model each sampling method with a school-of-1,000 example. Identify bias types (undercoverage, nonresponse, voluntary response, wording). Today's task from the plan: Compare simple random, stratified, cluster, and convenience samples; identify bias. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How is stratified sampling different from cluster sampling?
questions.a: Stratified: divide into groups and randomly sample from EVERY group. Cluster: divide into groups, randomly pick some whole groups, and survey everyone in them.

questions.q: An online poll on a sports site asks readers to vote. Main bias?
questions.a: Voluntary response bias: people with strong opinions choose to respond.

days.guide: Student writes a design: question, treatments, random assignment method, control, replication, and what to measure. Today's task from the plan: Design a randomized experiment testing whether music affects reaction time. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Why randomize in the music/reaction-time experiment?
questions.a: To balance unknown variables (sleep, skill) between groups so differences can be attributed to music.

days.guide: Student reads two articles and writes an evaluation: study type, sample, possible bias, and whether the headline's claim is justified. Today's task from the plan: Critique two news articles reporting on data; write an evaluation. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: A headline says 'Eating breakfast causes better grades' based on a survey. Is this justified?
questions.a: No. A survey is observational; confounding variables (family routines, income, sleep) could explain the association.

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz on study design and bias. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What is a confounding variable?
questions.a: A variable related to both the explanatory and response variables that makes it impossible to separate their effects.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) classify 5 scenarios (survey/experiment/observational). 2) name sampling method in 4 scenarios (SRS, stratified, cluster, convenience). 3) identify bias in a mall survey: undercoverage/convenience. 4) design rubric: random assignment (1), control/comparison group (1), replication (1), clear response variable (1). 5) Explain why causation cannot be concluded from an observational study.

weeks.prep: A data set of about 100 values (measure hand spans of family/friends or use published heights). Desmos normal distribution tool or a calculator with normalcdf.
misconceptions: Applying the 68-95-99.7 rule to skewed data. Check the histogram shape first.
Comparing raw scores across different tests. Convert to z-scores to compare relative standing.

days.guide: Make a histogram of the data set; describe shape, center, spread, and outliers. Today's task from the plan: Make histograms of a real data set (e.g., 100 measured hand spans) and describe shape. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: What does 'approximately normal' look like?
questions.a: Single-peaked, symmetric, bell-shaped, with mean ≈ median and few extreme values.

days.guide: Draw a normal curve with mean and ±1, 2, 3 SD marked; shade regions. Today's task from the plan: Apply the 68-95-99.7 rule to estimate percentages. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: IQ scores: mean 100, SD 15. What percent lie between 85 and 115? Above 130?
questions.a: About 68% (±1 SD). Above 130 is beyond +2 SD: about 2.5%.

days.guide: Model z = (x − μ)/σ. Compare two test results. Today's task from the plan: Calculate and compare z-scores (e.g., comparing ACT and SAT performance). Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: SAT 1300 (mean 1050, SD 200) vs ACT 28 (mean 21, SD 5). Which is better relative to peers?
questions.a: SAT z = 1.25; ACT z = 1.4. The ACT score is relatively better.

days.guide: Use technology to find areas; discuss when the normal model is inappropriate (skewed incomes, wait times). Today's task from the plan: Use technology to find areas under the normal curve; recognize when a normal model is not appropriate. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: With mean 100 and SD 10, find P(X > 120).
Find P(Z < 1).

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz on normal distributions. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: A z-score of −1.5 means what?
questions.a: The value is 1.5 standard deviations below the mean.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key (mean 70, SD 8): 1) % between 62 and 78 ≈ 68%. 2) % above 86 ≈ 2.5%. 3) z for 82 = 1.5. 4) P(X < 82) ≈ 0.9332. 5) P(66 < X < 74) ≈ 0.383. 6) Explain why house prices are not normally distributed (right-skewed). 1 pt each.

weeks.prep: Coins, dice, and a spreadsheet with =RAND() or =RANDBETWEEN(). Find a current poll with a margin of error.
misconceptions: Interpreting a margin of error as covering all possible errors. It accounts only for random sampling variability, not biased questions or samples.
Thinking a single unusual result proves unfairness. Compare the result with the spread of many simulated results.

days.guide: Flip a coin 50 times and count heads. In a spreadsheet, simulate 100 sets of 50 fair flips and make a dot plot of head counts. Today's task from the plan: Flip a coin 50 times; simulate 100 sets in a spreadsheet to judge whether results are consistent with fairness. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: If you got 32 heads in 50 flips, is the coin likely unfair?
questions.a: With a fair coin, 32 or more heads happens only about 3% of the time, so 32 is unusual and gives some evidence the coin is unfair (but is not proof).

days.guide: Simulate 200 samples of size 50 from a population with p = 0.40; plot the sample proportions. Today's task from the plan: Simulate many samples of size 50 from a known population proportion and plot proportions. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Describe the distribution of sample proportions.
questions.a: Centered near 0.40, roughly bell-shaped, with most proportions within about ±0.14 (2 SD, since SD = √(0.4·0.6/50) ≈ 0.069).

days.guide: Estimate the margin of error as about 2 SD from the simulation and compare with 1/√n. Today's task from the plan: Estimate margin of error from simulation and compare to 1/√n. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: What is the approximate margin of error for n = 400? For n = 1,000?

days.guide: Use random numbers to pick fairly (e.g., chores); analyze a game strategy with simulation. Today's task from the plan: Use random number generators to make fair decisions and analyze strategies. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How would you use a die to choose fairly among three people?
questions.a: Assign 1–2, 3–4, 5–6 to each person; each has probability 1/3.

days.guide: Give the quiz on interpreting margins of error (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz interpreting a poll's margin of error. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: A poll says 52% support a measure, ±3%. Can you conclude a majority supports it?
questions.a: No. The plausible range is 49%–55%, which includes values below 50%.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) 45% ±4% → plausible 41%–49%. 2) Quadrupling n halves the margin of error. 3) n = 2,500 → MOE ≈ 2%. 4) Explain why a self-selected online poll's margin of error is meaningless (bias). 5) Simulation shows 18–32 heads covers about 95% of fair 50-flip results; decide whether 35 heads is unusual (yes).

weeks.prep: Index cards for shuffling data. Materials for the chosen experiment (paper for airplanes, measuring tape) — let the student choose by Day 2.
misconceptions: Concluding 'no effect' when a difference isn't significant. It means the data don't give convincing evidence, not proof of no difference.
Running all trials of one treatment first (e.g., when tired). Randomize the order of trials.

days.guide: Write each result from a two-group experiment on a card; shuffle into two piles many times and record the difference in means. Compare to the actual difference.

questions.q: If only 2 of 100 shuffles give a difference as large as observed, what do you conclude?
questions.a: About 2% chance by random assignment alone, so the difference is statistically significant (unlikely to be due to chance).

days.guide: Student writes question, two treatments, response variable, randomization plan, and controlled variables. Today's task from the plan: Design a randomized experiment with two treatments (e.g., paper airplane wing design) and collect data. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Name three variables to hold constant in a paper-airplane experiment.
questions.a: Paper type and size, launcher and launch force/angle, and location (indoors, no wind).

days.guide: Run at least 20 trials per treatment in random order; record carefully. Today's task from the plan: Run the experiment with at least 20 trials per treatment. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Why at least 20 trials per treatment?
questions.a: Replication reduces the effect of chance variation so a real difference is easier to detect.

days.guide: Compute means, medians, and SDs; run a randomization test (spreadsheet or by hand with many shuffles). Today's task from the plan: Analyze results with a randomization test and summary statistics. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What does the p-value from the randomization test mean in your project?
questions.a: The proportion of random re-shuffles giving a difference at least as large as observed: the chance of seeing this difference if the treatment had no effect.

days.guide: Collect the report and give the Unit 9 test (about 45 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Submit a statistics project report and take the Unit 9 test. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Why can a well-designed randomized experiment show causation?
questions.a: Random assignment balances other variables, so a significant difference can be attributed to the treatment.

weeks.assessment_key: Project rubric (4 levels): design (randomization, control, replication), data quality (≥20 per treatment), analysis (summary stats + randomization test), conclusion (answers question, states uncertainty and limitations). Proficient = clear design, correct statistics, and a conclusion that does not overclaim. Unit 9 test sample answers: experiment vs observational identification; z = (85−75)/5 = 2; 95% within 2 SD; MOE ≈ 1/√n; interpretation of a p-value of 0.30 → not significant.

weeks.prep: Help the student find a public data set: California Department of Finance population, NOAA monthly temperatures, etc. Desmos.
misconceptions: Choosing the model with the best R² even if it makes absurd predictions. A model must also make sense in context (e.g., population can't go negative).
Extrapolating far outside the data range. Discuss how uncertainty grows beyond the data.

days.guide: Student picks a data set of 15+ points and graphs it in Desmos, writing what pattern they see. Today's task from the plan: Choose a real data set and graph it. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: What pattern would you expect in 12 months of average temperatures?

days.guide: Fit linear, quadratic, exponential, and sinusoidal regressions; plot residuals for each. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What does a good residual plot look like?
questions.a: Residuals scattered randomly around 0 with no curve or pattern.

days.guide: Student writes a one-page justification: chosen model, evidence (residuals, context), and limitations. Today's task from the plan: Write a justification for the best model, including limitations. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why might an exponential model fail for long-term population predictions?
questions.a: Resources limit growth; real populations level off (logistic), so exponential overpredicts.

days.guide: Student prepares a 5-minute presentation with a graph, model equation, predictions, and limits. Rehearse once. Today's task from the plan: Prepare a 5-minute presentation of the model and predictions. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What should every prediction slide include?
questions.a: The input value, predicted output with units, and a statement of confidence/limitations.

days.guide: Student presents; you ask two questions about model choice and limits. Today's task from the plan: Present the capstone and answer questions. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Your model predicts a value 30 years ahead. How confident should we be?
questions.a: Not very: extrapolation far beyond the data assumes the pattern continues, which is uncertain.

weeks.assessment_key: Capstone rubric (4 levels per row): Data (relevant, cited source, 15+ points); Models (at least 3 fitted, equations stated); Justification (residuals and context used to choose, limitations stated); Predictions (reasonable, within or near data range, with units); Presentation (clear, 5 minutes, answers questions). Proficient (3) = all rows present and correct with minor gaps.

weeks.prep: Final review packet (Khan Academy course challenge works well). Two quiet 60-minute exam blocks.
misconceptions: Spending review time only on favorite topics. Use the semester exam and quiz errors to target weak units.
Skipping the reflection. Error analysis is where most learning from an exam happens.

days.guide: Mixed review on Units 1–5; student marks unsure items to revisit. Today's task from the plan: Mixed review on quadratics, polynomials, rationals, and radicals. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Solve √(x + 5) = x − 1.

days.guide: Mixed review on Units 6–9. Today's task from the plan: Mixed review on exponentials, logs, trig, sequences, and statistics. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Solve 5e^(2t) = 40.
Find the sum of the infinite series 9 + 3 + 1 + ….

days.guide: Final part 1: non-calculator (60 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Non-calculator section. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Evaluate log₃81 + sin(π/6).

days.guide: Final part 2: calculator and modeling (60 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Calculator section with modeling tasks. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: $3,000 at 5% compounded monthly; when does it reach $5,000?

days.guide: Return the graded exam; student writes a reflection on each missed item and on readiness for Precalculus. Today's task from the plan: Review exam errors and write a reflection on growth and readiness for Precalculus. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What should an error reflection include?
questions.a: The item, what went wrong (concept vs careless), the correct solution, and one action to prevent it.

weeks.assessment_key: Final exam representative answers: (x−3)²+2 vertex (3,2); 2x²+7x+3 = (2x+1)(x+3); x³−6x²+11x−6 zeros 1, 2, 3; (x+1)/(x²−1) = 1/(x−1); 16^(3/4)=8; log₂(x)=5 → 32; cos(5π/3)=1/2; period of 3 sin(2x) is π; a₁₀ of 2, 6, 18 is 39,366; 95% of normal data within 2 SD. Grade bands: 90%+ excellent, 75–89% proficient, 60–74% basic (review before Precalculus), below 60% needs targeted summer work. Reflection rubric: complete error analysis for every missed item = full credit.
